claims.text: The single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu coating is initially a stable FCC phase with low dislocation density at 300 K.
Above 900 K, thermally activated stacking-fault annihilation initiates the proposed microstructural cascade.
Stacking-fault annihilation is followed by rapid amorphization of the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Amorphization and dislocation starvation eliminate the dislocation-mediated plasticity needed for energy dissipation.
Loss of dislocation-mediated plasticity produces brittle-like adhesive wear.
The FCC-to-amorphous transition is mediated by annihilation of Shockley partial dislocations and collapse of stacking faults.
Stacking-fault collapse causes a loss of HCP stacking sequences and total dislocation line length.
Above 900 K, thermal energy exceeds the relevant stacking-fault energy barrier.
Exceeding the stacking-fault energy barrier causes rapid annihilation of Shockley partials and dislocation starvation.
The FCC lattice collapses into a disordered amorphous phase between approximately 900 K and 1200 K.
Amorphization prevents formation of stable shear bands.
The lack of a protective work-hardened layer promotes adhesive transfer or galling.
Adhesive transfer causes a spike in friction and increased wear.
The coefficient of friction and wear rate increase sharply above 900 K.
The friction and wear transition is accompanied by a measurable decrease in HCP atom count.
The friction and wear transition is accompanied by a precipitous decrease in total dislocation line length.
At 600 K, a slight reduction in dislocation density increases the elastic modulus without causing significant amorphization.
The coating maintains stable friction and wear resistance at 300 K and 600 K.
Polycrystalline variants may instead be dominated by grain-boundary sliding.
Artificially increasing stacking-fault energy will inhibit partial-dislocation annihilation under otherwise identical thermal conditions.
